evidence.text:
Controlled Polymerization of β‑Pinadiene: Accessing Unusual
Polymer Architectures with Biomass-Derived Monomers
Alan D. Fried and Johnathan N. Brantley *
Cite This: ACS Macro Lett. 2020, 9, 595 −599 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: Biomass-derived polymers are emerging as critically
needed alternatives to their petrochemical counterparts. Terpenes,
which are among the most abundant natural products, represent
particularly fertile chemical space for monomer development
(given their inherent structural complexity). Here, we present the
living vinyl-addition polymerization of β-pinadiene (the cumulated
congener of β-pinene) at room temperature. Employing [( π-
allyl)NiOCOCF
3]2 as a catalyst a ﬀorded the desired polymers with
good control over molecular weight and dispersity. Interestingly,
the bicyclic pinane core was retained in the isolated materials
(which starkly contrasts prototypical pinene polymerizations).
Moreover, the reported materials exhibited impressive thermal
stability (T
d = 294 °C) and high glass transition temperatures ( Tg
= 160 °C). As the polymerization of terpene-derived cumulenes can a ﬀord scaﬀolds that defy current synthetic logic, we anticipate
our work will unlock additional avenues for sustainable polymer development.
A
s the demand for commodity plastics has increased, so
too has global production of synthetic polymers. 1 Nearly
350 Mt of these materials are generated every year, 2 and over
40% of these polymers are polyole ﬁns.2 As polyole ﬁns are
predominantly derived from petrochemical feedstocks, their
preparation on such a scale necessitates signi ﬁcant oil
consumption. Indeed, nearly 10% of crude oil production is
diverted to polymer manufacturing (a ﬁgure that is expected to
double by 2050).
3 The rising demand for polyole ﬁns starkly
contrasts the availability of the raw materials for their
production; thus, the development of more sustainable
alternatives is imperative. Biological feedstocks o ﬀer a rich
diversity of potential monomers (both in terms of chemical
functionality and structural complexity), and they are
increasingly becoming focal points for advancements in
polymer science. For example, polylactide is a commercially
viable alternative to polyethylene and polystyrene in certain
applications.4,5 Biobased diamines and dicarboxylic acids have
also emerged as precursors for polyamides used in the
automotive6 and medical industries. 7 As such, the investigation
of novel, biologically derived monomers is essential for
realizing next-generation renewable materials.
Terpenes, which are common plant oils, have been
investigated as monomers since the early 20th century,
8 and
synthetic polyterpenes have found a myriad of uses (e.g., as
tackiﬁers,9 adhesives,10 food packaging materials, 11 and latex
substitutes12). Pinenes are particularly promising candidates
for renewable monomers, given their high natural abundance. 13
While both α- and β-pinene undergo polymerization, β-pinene
reacts more readily due to facile ring opening (and
concomitant relief of ring strain). 14
While cationic polymerization is the most reliable method
for preparing poly( β-pinene),15 this approach su ﬀers from
several limitations. For example, high catalyst loadings and
incremental monomer additions are common requisites.
Cryogenic conditions are also typical, although Lu and co-
workers recently disclosed the polymerization of β-pinene to
modest number-average molecular weight ( M
n = 10 900 Da) at
elevated temperatures. 16 Moreover, the preparation of
polymers with high molecular weight ( Mn > 50 000 Da) has
proven challenging. In fact, the ﬁrst synthesis of a relatively
high Mn (cf. 50 000 Da) pinene polymer was only recently
disclosed by Kamigaito et al. 17 The team reported a living
polymerization mediated by EtAlCl 2, but incremental mono-
mer addition and cryogenic temperatures were required to
achieve good conversion. Additionally, the catalyst exhibited
apparent deactivation at longer reaction times. As such,
opportunities remain for improving access to pinene-derived
polymers.

We became intrigued by β-pinene as a monomer not only
because of its relative abundance but also because of the
bicyclic nature of the pinane core. The incorporation of rigid
carbocycles into polymers can dramatically alter bulk proper-
ties,
18−22 but there have been no reports detailing materials
that contain a pinane motif. As traditional polymerizations of
β-pinene proceed with concomitant destruction of the pinane
bicycle,
14,17,23,24 we sought to develop an alternative strategy
that would circumvent t his reactivity. Speci ﬁcally, we
hypothesized that retention of the bicyclic system would be
possible if propagating intermediates were isolated on exocyclic
positions.
Extending the ole ﬁn through cumulation could potentially
enable such a scenario, especially if the cumulene exhibited
selective 2,3-polymerization tendencies. Allenes are known to
polymerize under a variety of conditions (e.g., radical
25 or
coordination−insertion26−28), but these approaches typically
exhibit poor regioselectivity. Endo, however, has demonstrated
that hindered, 1,1-disubstit uted allenes undergo living
polymerizations with excellent selectivity for 2,3-insertions in
the presence of a ( π-allyl)Ni catalyst ( 4, Scheme 1 ).
29 We
envisioned that the pinane core would be su ﬃciently
encumbering to promote exclusive 2,3-polymerization under
the action of Endo ’s catalyst. Furthermore, we hypothesized
that selective 2,3-polymerization of β-pinadiene would
preclude ring opening; thus, we could potentially interrogate
polymer properties associated with this repeating unit.
Our investigation began with the synthesis of β-pinadiene
monomer, 2. Treatment of (1 S)-(−)-β-pinene with bromo-
form and KOH under phase transfer conditions smoothly
aﬀorded 1 in excellent yield (93%; Scheme 1 ; see the
Supporting Information for additional details). We found this
reaction could be conducted on a decagram scale without the
need for tedious puri ﬁcation strategies. Under the action of
MeLi, 1 undergoes a Skattebøl rearrangement
30 to a ﬀord 2,
which could be isolated in good yield (85%) following
distillation. Moreover, neat samples of 2 could be stored
indeﬁnitely at −20 °C.
Given the enhanced regioselectivity reported by Endo,
29 we
elected to use vinyl-addition catalyst 4 in an initial polymer-
ization attempt ( Table 1 ; entry 1). Quantitative consumption
of 2 in toluene was observed after 70 min (as determined by
1H NMR spectroscopy), at which point the reaction mixture
was added to MeOH to precipitate any polymeric material.
Filtration a ﬀorded 3 as a white powder in excellent yield
(93%). The polymer was analyzed by gel permeation
chromatography (GPC), which revealed an M
n value in good
agreement with the theoretical value (cf. 39 210 Da versus 30
000 Da) and narrow dispersity ( Đ = 1.16). Although we
surveyed other common vinyl addition catalysts (precatalyst 5,
and 6; Scheme 1 ; SI), neither outperformed 4 (Table 1 ).
1H NMR spectroscopic analysis of the material prepared
using catalyst 4 was consistent with the expected 2,3-
regioselectivity, given the absence of observable vinyl
resonances ( Figure 1 ). Importantly, however, these data also
suggested the retention of the bicyclic pinane core. Indeed,
ring opening of this motif would be expected to a ﬀord a new
vinylic signal from the associated endocyclic ole ﬁn( vide inf ra).
To further investigate the material ’s structure, we performed a
series of correlational and heteronuclear single quantum
coherence (HSQC)
13C−1H NMR spectroscopy experiments.
To our delight, these data con ﬁrmed the 13C resonances
associated with the pinane bridgehead methines (cf. 46.4 and
40.7 ppm) and methylenes (cf. 28.2, 24.7, and 21.8 ppm) were
retained in the polymer ( Figure 1 ; Figures S19, S20, S23, and
S24).
Having established the superior reactivity of 4, we sought to
further optimize the polymerization conditions. 4 performed
poorly in acetonitrile, a ﬀording only 14% conversion of 2 after
70 min (as determined by
1H NMR spectroscopy; Table 1 ).
Tetrahydrofuran improved monomer conversion, but the
isolated polymer exhibited broad dispersity and a calculated
M
n value that far exceeded the target (as determined by GPC;
Table 1 ). Conversely, diethyl ether improved control over Mn
and Đ, but overall monomer conversion was reduced.
Polymerizations conducted in dichloromethane or toluene
reached full conversion within 70 min, and the M
n values
determined by GPC were typically in good agreement with the

theoretical values ( Table 1 ). Toluene was ultimately selected
as solvent, however, as it a ﬀorded lower dispersity materials.
We also explored the polymerization of 2 under other
conditions, but we note that vinyl-addition proved to be the
most successful strategy. Cationic polymerization mediated by
various Lewis acids (e.g., AlCl
3) proved ine ﬀectual (or resulted
in ring opening, as evidenced by two sets of vinyl resonances in
the 1H NMR spectrum; Table S2 ; Figure S27 ). Moreover,
neither radical nor anionic polymerizations a ﬀorded any
polymeric material ( SI).
Using our chosen conditions, we successfully prepared
materials exhibiting a wide range of molecular weights ( Mn =
7504−99 580 Da; Đ = 1.13 −1.37) in excellent yields (87 −
99%; Table 2). We note that preparation of high Mn materials
(>60 000 Da) necessitated more dilute concentrations ([ 2]0 ≤
0.10 M) in order to prevent gelation prior to full conversion.
To assess the living character of these polymerizations, we
monitored M
n as a function of monomer conversion ( SI). The
observed linear correlation, combined with a consistently low
dispersity ( Đ < 1.30), provided strong evidence that the
polymerization was living ( Figure 2 A). This conclusion was
further corroborated through chain-extension experiments
(Figure 2 B). Brie ﬂy, the polymerization was monitored by
1H NMR spectroscopy until complete consumption of 2 was
observed. An aliquot of the reaction was removed and analyzed
by GPC (following drying under high vacuum). A subsequent
portion of 2 was then added to the reaction mixture. Upon
consumption of the added monomer, an aliquot was removed
and analyzed by GPC. This process was repeated an additional
time, and GPC analyses of all three materials were consistent
with ﬁdelitous chain extension ( Figure 2 B). This living
character starkly contrasts previous reports of pinene polymer-
izations, and the ability to chain extend 3 could facilitate the
incorporation of pinane motifs into a broader range of soft
materials.
Having synthesized our target materials, we sought to
interrogate some of their bulk properties. For comparison, we
also prepared a polymer from (1 S)-(−)-β-pinene using
standard
23 cationic conditions ( 7; Mn = 5812 Da; Đ = 1.91;
Scheme 1 ; SI). Thermogravimetric analysis of both materials
revealed similar decomposition onset temperatures (cf. Td =
294 °C for 3 versus 303 °C for 7; Figures S6 and S8 ,
respectively). Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) of powder
samples revealed striking dissimilarities between 3 and 7.
While 3 exhibited a T
g = 160 °C (determined using tan( δ)max;
Figure S7), 7 exhibited a signi ﬁcantly lower Tg =8 2 °C (which
was consistent with previous reports; 23 Figure S9). As such, we
expected 3 to exhibit some rigidi ﬁcation (i.e., crystallinity). To
investigate, we performed wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS)
on two di ﬀerent samples of 3 (M
n = 7504 and 79 910 Da).
Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed two semicrystal-

line peaks (average 2 θ = 7.45 ° and 15.52 °) in both samples
(Figures S10 and S11 ). To ascertain if these data were
associated with metastable phases, we annealed a sample of 3
(Mn = 66 090 Da) for 1 h under vacuum ( SI). WAXS analysis
of the annealed polymer was similar to the virgin material,
albeit with larger average crystallite sizes ( Figure S12 ; Table
S3). In contrast, WAXS analysis of 7 revealed a peak at 2 θ =
7.52° (which disappeared upon annealing; Figure S14 ) and
another semicrystalline peak at 2 θ = 15.74 ° (Figure S13 ).
Moreover, the interchain d-spacing for annealed samples of 3
was smaller than that of annealed samples of 7 (cf. 11.46 versus
13.92 nm, respectively; Tables S3 and S4 ). Although
preliminary, these data suggest that 3 exhibits tighter packing
than 7. Additional studies are currently underway to gain a
deeper understanding of the morphologies associated with
these polymers.
In conclusion, we have demonstrated that cumulation is a
powerful strategy for accessing unique polymer architectures
from biomass-derived monomers. The terpene congener, β-
pinadiene, can be prepared in two steps on a multigram scale
without the need for extensive puri ﬁcation. Vinyl-addition
polymerization of this monomer is rapid at room temperature,
exhibits living character, and a ﬀords high M
n materials with low
dispersity. Importantly, these unique polymers retain their
pinane core structure, and they exhibit physical properties that
contrast those of poly( β-pinene). We believe this work
presents a new opportunity to probe biomass-derived polymers
and explore untapped chemical space in renewable polymer
technology.
